title: Social cognition and parenting among Black caregivers: Linking public regard to racial and emotion socialization.
abstract: Among Black families, cultural racism necessitates adaptations in emotion socialization to prepare children for navigating racialized environments. Black caregivers with high negative public regard, or the belief that others view Black Americans negatively, may engage in racial barrier socialization and discourage their children's expression of negative emotions. However, no studies have directly tested associations among negative public regard, racial barrier socialization, and emotion socialization practices. The present study employed a social-cognitive framework to examine direct and indirect associations between negative public regard, racial barrier socialization, and suppressive emotion socialization practices among Black caregivers. It was hypothesized that negative public regard would be associated with higher racial barrier socialization and, in turn, greater use of distress, minimizing, and punitive emotion socialization practices. Black caregivers (= 100;= 43.57 years,= 7.75; 91% female) completed self-report measures of racial identity, racial socialization, discrimination, and emotion socialization. Controlling for child sex, caregiver emotion dysregulation, and prior discrimination experiences, we found a significant indirect effect of negative public regard on minimizing (but not punitive nor distress) emotion socialization through racial barrier socialization. These findings incrementally advance extant literature, which contends that Black caregivers' racial barrier socialization and minimizing emotion socialization may operate in tandem to prepare Black youth for others' negative prejudicial beliefs and anti-Black racism in broader society.
